How cognitive AI learns

Is there a right answer to check against?

Supervised

Learns from past loans with known outcomes. Where the 3.4% comes from.

Unsupervised

No labels. Finds structure and outliers: "Vindrø's payments look unlike its peers'."

Reinforcement

Acts, observes a reward, adjusts. Pricing round after round in ProBanker. Rare in production.

Only supervised learning has a right answer for every case. That is where precision and recall work.
RECAP ONLY, 3 minutes: students read §13.2. Supervised = a teacher gives the answers. Unsupervised = no teacher. Reinforcement = a coach saying warmer/colder. Ch 13 §13.2.

One number for both · F1

Balancing precision and recall

F1  =  2×Precision×RecallPrecision+Recall  =  2×0.28×0.700.28+0.70  =  0.40F_1 \;=\; \frac{2 \times \text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}} \;=\; \frac{2 \times 0.28 \times 0.70}{0.28 + 0.70} \;=\; 0.40
A good recall can't hide a bad precision. F1 drags the score toward the weaker one.
Keep it simple. Precision (28%, Team Growth's number) and recall (70%, Team Prudence's) sit at the two ends of a seesaw. On landing: equal weights, so it balances in the middle, the simple average, 49%. Click 1: F1 gives the weaker score the heavier weight, so the balance point slides toward precision: 40%. (That is exactly what the formula does: it is a weighted average in which each measure is weighted by the other one.) Click 2: the formula. F1 is the elementary method, and its weights are fixed by the formula. Bridge aloud: "F1 weighs the two errors for you. Next, you weigh them yourself." After the threshold slider: the three questions banks ask, and the one we pick (AUC).
BOOK · §13.2.1
SLIDO · 2 of 5
F1 weighed the two errors for you · now weigh them yourself: k

How many good firms would you turn away to avoid one default?

k  =  cost of one defaultcost of one lost good customerk \;=\; \dfrac{\text{cost of one default}}{\text{cost of one lost good customer}}
Decline when PD>11+k\text{PD} > \dfrac{1}{1+k}
Launch Slido 2 of 5 and type the counts into the boxes; the class median appears under the bars. The fear ratio k is a cost ratio: the cost of lending to a firm that defaults divided by the cost of turning away a firm that would repay. Say it once: "fear" is the nickname, the ratio is what we measure. The ladder asks the same thing as an exchange rate: how many lost customers is one default worth? Click once: the curve converts any k into a cut-off and plots the class. ★ AHA #3 (pause here). My fear has a number, and the bank's is 32 against my 2. | Decision rule: decline if PD × cost of a default > (1 − PD) × cost of turning a good firm away. With k = cost ratio, the break-even PD is 1/(1+k). Lab studies put human loss aversion at about 2 (Tversky & Kahneman 1992; prospect theory, Kahneman & Tversky 1979): a loss weighs about twice an equal gain. That is an analogy for k, not the same quantity: it compares losing with gaining money, while k compares two kinds of error. The bank's 3.0% policy implies k ≈ 32. Banks are far more "fearful" than human psychology. Why: the capped-upside slide, after the ROC curve. Straight after the k echoes, the threshold slider puts the room's cut-off to work.
Every field has a k

How many cheap mistakes to avoid one expensive one?

Your bank is three times harsher on borrowers than Blackstone was on criminals.
k as an exchange rate between two mistakes. The axis is logarithmic. Click 1: you. In the lab, a loss weighs about twice an equal gain (Tversky & Kahneman 1992); the room's ladder median sits above the line. Click 2: the law has argued about its k for centuries. Blackstone (Commentaries, 1769): better ten guilty escape than one innocent suffer. Franklin (letter to Benjamin Vaughan, 1785): a hundred. Maimonides (Sefer HaMitzvot, negative commandment 290): a thousand. Volokh, "n Guilty Men", U. Penn. Law Review 146 (1997), surveys the rest. Click 3: the bank's own AML desk; at 5–15% precision it accepts about nine false alerts per launderer caught. Click 4: the credit policy. A 3.0% cut-off means k ≈ 32: 32 good firms turned away per default avoided. Ask: who chose 32, and did anyone write it down? That question is the board's job (synthesis map, Session 4).

Beyond F1 · how banks grade a PD model

F1 is the textbook balance. Banks ask three questions.

What we just did

F1

One cut-off, one number. Common for alert systems (fraud, AML). Rare for PD models: it ignores the correctly approved and picks a cut-off for you.

Discrimination

Does it rank?

Are the defaulters scored riskier than the good firms?

ROC curve · AUCGini · accuracy ratioKS statistic
Calibration

Is 3.4% really 3.4%?

Do firms scored 3.4% default about 3.4% of the time?

Binomial / Jeffreys testTraffic-light back-testBrier score
Stability

Does it still fit?

Are today's applicants like the loans it learned from?

Stability index (PSI)Drift checks
Validation reports answer all three. We take the one you'll meet in every report: AUC. None of the three sets the cut-off: k does.
F1 was the elementary balance between precision and recall. Banks grade PD models differently, and supervisors expect three questions answered. Discrimination: does the model rank defaulters above good firms? (ROC/AUC, its twin Gini or accuracy ratio, the KS statistic.) Calibration: is a 3.4% PD really 3.4%? (binomial or Jeffreys tests of realised default rates, traffic-light back-tests, Brier score.) Stability: does the applicant pool still look like the training data? (population stability index, drift monitoring: Session 3.) F1 belongs to alert systems such as fraud and AML screening, where one cut-off is fixed. Click: we pick AUC, because it is in every validation report and because it grades the ranking without choosing a cut-off; the cut-off is k, the board's call. Verify the supervisor reference before class (ECB validation reporting asks for AUC, a Jeffreys calibration test and stability checks).
BOOK · §13.2.1
Discrimination · the one we pick

Every cut-off at once: the ROC curve

ROC = receiver operating characteristic, a name from Second World War radar: how well an operator told aircraft from noise.

Across: share of good firms wrongly rejected (false-positive rate)

Up: share of defaulters caught (recall)

Each point is one cut-off. Moving the slider walks you along the curve.

Diagonal = a coin. Reject 30% at random, catch 30% of defaulters.

AUC = the whole shaded area under the curve. 0.5 is a coin, 1.0 is perfect. Also: the chance the model ranks a random defaulter riskier than a random good firm.

Gini = 2 × AUC − 1: the gap between the curve and the coin. It's the number most bank validation reports quote.

AUC grades the model across every cut-off. Picking the cut-off is still the board's job.
The method picked from the previous slide. The threshold slider moved one point at a time; the ROC curve draws every cut-off at once. Start with the diagonal: a coin that rejects firms at random catches defaulters in proportion, so it sits on the 45° line. Click 1: our model's curve, with the policy cut-off marked (catches 70% of defaulters, wrongly rejects 7.5% of good firms). Click 2: AUC is the entire area under the curve, not just the part above the diagonal; a coin scores 0.5. Click 3: the area between the curve and the diagonal, doubled, is the Gini coefficient (accuracy ratio), Gini = 2·AUC − 1, the number most bank model validation reports. Banks like AUC/Gini because it grades the ranking without committing to a cut-off; the cut-off is k, which is a policy choice. Calibration and stability, the other two questions, are named on the previous slide; calibration is drawn in the appendix.
BOOK · §13.2.1
Why banks are so afraid

A lender's upside is capped. Its downside isn't.

The bank's fear is not psychology. It is arithmetic.
SET PIECE: tell it straight, no interaction. ★ AHA #4 (pause here). A lender's upside is capped; its downside isn't. The bank's fear is arithmetic. | Lender earns the margin (≈2.5% a year) if Vindrø does well, and loses up to ≈40% of the exposure if it fails. The founders' upside is open-ended. That asymmetry is why k ≈ 32 is rational for a lender and k ≈ 2 is rational-ish for a gambler.
Vindrø in DKK · illustrative

Expected loss is a cost. Capital is a cushion.

Pricing pays for the average year. Capital pays for the bad one. One firm can't show you the bad year; a thousand can.
Keep Basel to intuition: no formula, no risk weights. Every number has a hover tooltip with its calculation. On landing, one Vindrø: expected loss 3.4% × 40% × DKK 8 m ≈ 109k a year, a cost built into the price like an insurance premium. Capital: 15% × DKK 8 m = DKK 1.2 m of the bank's own equity, locked up for as long as the loan is on the books, eleven times the annual expected loss. The bank pays rent on it (10% cost of equity ≈ 120k a year), which is the capital bar on the next slide. Click 1: lend to 1,000 firms like Vindrø. On average 34 default a year and the loss (≈ DKK 109 m) is in the price. Lending to many firms removes one firm's bad luck, not a recession, when firms default together, hence the long right tail. Most years are better than average (median ≈ 26 defaults); the bad years pull the average up. Click 2: one year in twenty, 90 or more default (think 2009): DKK 289 m lost. Pricing covers 109 m; capital absorbs the other 180 m. That is what the capital is for, and why the bank's k ≈ 32: it reasons about the tail, not the average. For the curious: regulators size capital for a far rarer year (roughly one in a thousand, about 210 defaults here); the 1.2 m also includes buffers. Illustrative one-factor model, correlation 0.12, LGD 40%, fully drawn line.

The choice is not approve/decline: it is price, structure, or walk away. Simplified (no SME supporting factor, fully drawn line). Links: Ch 6 risk-adjusted performance, Ch 12 capital.

85–95% false-positive rates: precision 5–15%

Too many alarms and people stop reading. One confident alarm and they stop thinking.

DISCUSS
AI across the commercial bank

Where banks use AI vs where it works

Ask first, with only the empty axes on screen: where would you put fraud detection? The customer chatbot? Then one click per quadrant. 1 · Working: fraud, credit scoring, KYC and onboarding checks, marketing and next-best offer. The outcome is observed fast and in volume (a fraud, a default, a forged ID, a click), so the model is checked and improved. 2 · Ahead of the evidence: customer chatbots, AML transaction monitoring, GenAI copilots (memos, code). Widely deployed, but the benefit is hard to measure or the error rate is high (AML false positives; the wrong memo from Session 3). 3 · Under-used: collections, liquidity and deposit forecasting, loan and deposit pricing. The models work; banks lag because of validation skills, legacy data, and who owns the decision (bank-side treasury lags corporate treasury, §13.7). 4 · Not yet: agentic end-to-end lending and advice. The pieces have to work together first. 5 · The reveal: it is the approval machine again. The bank decides yes or no on each AI project; the truth is whether the AI works. Teal = correctly adopted; orange = wrongly adopted, Team Prudence's fear (losses, fines, complaints); blue = wrongly passed over, Team Growth's fear (a competitor gets there first); grey = correctly waiting. Ask: which team does your bank's AI strategy belong to? The pattern to land: AI works where the truth arrives quickly and in volume. Adoption follows the money and the vendors, not always the evidence. Placements are illustrative: adoption draws on Table 13.1 and industry surveys; effectiveness is our reading of the chapter. Say so.

BOOK · §13.11.4
ESG · the shape of it · §13.11

The same loop, with one wire missing

hover a box for detail
ESG is the credit loop without the defaults.
One structure, no acronyms on screen; the book is the reference. Every bank activity runs the same loop: commit, measure, act, report, and the world feeds back. On landing: the credit loop they know from today. Commit = risk appetite, the k. Measure = the PD. Act = lend, price, structure. Report. And the feedback is hard and fast: defaults tell you within a year if you were wrong. Click 1: the ESG loop, same four steps. The book's sections hang on these nodes; don't name them, just say "this is §13.11 on one page": Commit = responsible banking, the UN principles banks sign, the SDGs (Jyske signed). Measure = the E, S and G metrics and their problems. Act = green bonds, sustainability-linked loans, screening and exclusion, engagement. Report = integrated reporting and the EU reporting rules. Click 2: the difference is the feedback wire. In ESG the world reacts to the report, not to the truth: reputation, regulators, ratings, slowly. Ask: what happens to a loop whose feedback reacts to the report? (The report runs ahead of the substance: greenwashing.) Click 3: the weakest node is Measure. Next slide zooms into it.
BOOK · §13.11
ESG as measurement · §13.11.4

E, S and G are three different kinds of number

hover a point for detail
S behaves like credit risk. E is real but estimated. G is easy to count and hard to trust.
ESG in the language of the afternoon: how is it measured, and does the truth ever arrive to check it? Start with the reference point students know: PD, observed directly (defaults happen) and checkable within a year. Click 1, S: financial inclusion sits right next to PD. Approvals and defaults by group are counted, and the model can be calibrated by group (the Session 3 subgroup slide). Click 2, E: financed emissions are physically real but for SMEs mostly estimated from sector averages (PCAF data-quality score 4–5 out of 5); transition risk is further out still: scenarios, no backtest for decades (drift). Click 3, G: board composition and policies are easy to count today, but they measure paperwork; whether governance actually works shows up only in rare failures, like Danske Estonia, which is the accuracy trap again: a rare event makes "everyone is fine" look accurate. Click 4: an ESG rating mixes all three with weights, and there is no event to check it against; raters agree at 0.54 (Berg et al. 2022). The book's three ESG problems (data quality, no single standard, materiality) are all visible on this map.

DISCUSS
No shared target · Berg, Kölbel & Rigobon (2022)

Credit raters agree. ESG raters don't.

Six ESG raters:MSCIKLDSustainalyticsVigeo Eiris now Moody'sRobecoSAM now S&P GlobalAsset4 now LSEG
Why they disagree
Measurement 56%same issue, different yardstick
Scope 38%different issues counted
6%

The last 6% is weights: how much each issue counts.

Train an AI on rater A and it learns rater A. A PD predicts the world; an ESG score predicts the rater.
Ask first: "Rater A calls Vindrø a leader, rater B a laggard. Which one is wrong?" Then build. The numbers are correlations between two raters' scores for the same firms: 1 means they rank firms the same way, 0 means no relation. Moody's and S&P credit ratings correlate at 0.99 because both aim at the same observable event, default. The six ESG raters (MSCI, MSCI KLD, Sustainalytics, Vigeo Eiris, now Moody's ESG; RobecoSAM, now S&P Global; Asset4, now Refinitiv/LSEG) agree at 0.38–0.71, average 0.54. Click 2: the paper decomposes the disagreement: measurement (same category, different indicators) about 56%, scope (which categories count) about 38%, weights about 6%. Click 3: the AI point. A model trained on ESG ratings has no world to be right about, only a rater to imitate. Verify the decomposition shares and the 0.99 against the paper before class. Neither rater has to be wrong: they measure different things under one name.
Berg, Kölbel & Rigobon (2022), "Aggregate Confusion: The Divergence of ESG Ratings", Review of Finance 26(6). Correlation of two raters' scores across the same firms.

HANDS UP
One year later

Two endings. Was your decision right? Was the model wrong?

Ending A

Vindrø thrives

A second service contract. The line is renewed, priced and covenanted as agreed.

Ending B

The operator cancels

70% of revenue gone in a quarter. Vindrø defaults; the bank recovers about 60%.

Who would now change their vote?
Same file, same decision, two endings. Judge the decision by what you knew. Judge the model by calibration: of 100 firms like Vindrø at 2.7%, about 3 default.

If you declined, you never learn which ending was yours: the blind spot. If you lent, an agent watching Vindrø's account could have seen the cancellation coming months earlier.

Outcome bias. Reveal A, let the approvers enjoy it, then B. Ask for hands: who changes their vote now? Anyone who does is judging the decision by its outcome. One loan is one draw from the PD. The model is right or wrong only across many firms (calibration, appendix); the decision is right or wrong only given what was known at the time. Ending B is exactly the transition door: checkable later, never in advance.

The prediction. Not the fear, not the decision. Review Q1 · Q7

Review questions Q1 (adoption causes) and Q7 (find a product marketed as AI and test it) as homework. ★ AHA #10 (pause here). The AI owns the prediction. The board owns the fear and the definition. The banker owns the structure. | Answer to the "who should decide?" hand vote. The AI is a prediction machine; the fear ratio is a value judgment that belongs to the board's risk appetite; the structure is the banker's craft (Agrawal, Gans & Goldfarb, Prediction Machines, 2018). A vendor that claims to "learn your risk appetite" is claiming to own the board's job.

Appendix · validation

F1 picks a side. Banks use AUC and calibration.

F1 = harmonic mean of precision and recall. It weights FP and FN equally and ignores TN, so it quietly prefers one cut-off. Banks validate PD models with AUC / Gini, which scores ranking across all cut-offs, and calibration: do firms scored 3.4% default about 3.4% of the time? The ROC curve is the threshold slider drawn all at once. Calibration panel is illustrative.
Appendix · vocabulary 1 of 3

Words you met today

AI and learning
Automation (RPA)Software that repeats fixed steps. Follows rules; learns nothing.
Cognitive (predictive) AILearns patterns from past data to predict an outcome, such as a PD.
Generative AIProduces new text or images from a prompt, such as a credit memo.
Agentic AIChains steps and tools toward a goal, and can act on the result.
Supervised learningLearns from past cases whose outcomes are known (labels).
Training dataThe past cases a model learns from; it knows nothing else.
Measuring a model · 1
PDProbability of default: the chance a borrower defaults within a year.
Confusion matrix2 × 2 table of what the model said against what actually happened.
TP · TNThe right calls: a positive correctly flagged, a negative correctly cleared.
FP · FNThe wrong calls: a false alarm, and a miss.
Positive classThe outcome the machine is built to flag: reject, or approve.
Base rateThe share of cases that are actually positive, e.g. 4% default.
PrecisionTP / (TP + FP): of the cases flagged, the share that were right.
RecallTP / (TP + FN): of the true positives, the share caught.
F1Harmonic mean of precision and recall: one number that balances both.
Appendix · vocabulary 2 of 3

Words you met today

Measuring a model · 2
AccuracyShare of all calls that are right. Misleading when the event is rare.
Threshold (cut-off)The score above which the machine flags a case.
False-positive rateShare of true negatives wrongly flagged: good firms rejected.
ROC curveRecall against false-positive rate, across every threshold.
AUCArea under the ROC curve. 0.5 = a coin, 1.0 = perfect ranking.
Gini2 × AUC − 1: ranking power above random. Common in bank validation.
CalibrationWhether predicted PDs match realised default rates.
KS statisticThe largest gap between the score distributions of defaulters and good firms: another ranking measure.
Population stability indexHow far today's applicants have shifted from the data the model learned on.
Decision economics
Fear ratio kA cost ratio: cost of a default ÷ cost of turning away a good firm. "Fear" is the nickname.
Cut-off PD = 1 / (1 + k)The PD above which declining is the cheaper mistake.
Loss aversionLosses weigh about twice as much as equal gains.
Expected loss (EL)PD × LGD × EAD: the average loss priced into a loan.
LGDLoss given default: the share of the exposure lost if the borrower defaults.
Cost of capitalThe return owed on the equity a loan ties up.
Break-even marginThe margin at which a loan covers EL, capital and running costs.
Appendix · vocabulary 3 of 3

Words you met today

Failure modes
Reject inferenceEstimating how rejected applicants would have performed.
Blind spotErrors the bank can never observe: the good firms it turned away.
Subgroup disparityA model that is fine on average but worse for one group.
Indirect discriminationA neutral rule with an unequal effect on a protected group (US: disparate impact).
DriftThe world changes after training, and the model goes stale.
Alert fatigueSo many false alarms that reviewers stop reading them.
Adversarial adaptationThose being screened learn to evade the model.
Automation biasPeople defer to a machine's recommendation.
HallucinationGenerative AI stating something false with confidence.
AI washingOverstating, or inventing, the AI in a product.
Framing (label) effectA label changes judgment of identical facts.
Outcome biasJudging a decision by how it turned out, not by what was known.
Law and governance
EU AI ActEU law that regulates AI by risk level.
High-risk AI systemAn AI use, such as scoring individuals for credit, that requires documentation, oversight and bias testing.
ExplainabilityBeing able to give the reasons behind a model's output.
EU TaxonomyEU classification of environmentally sustainable activities.
Appendix · concepts 1 of 2

Ideas to take away

ConceptIn one lineSlide
Prediction vs judgmentAI supplies the prediction; people supply the values and the action.
Learning paradigmsOnly supervised learning has a right answer to check against.
Out-of-distribution riskA model is reliable only on cases like those it has seen.
Choice of positive classFP and FN swap names when the question is framed the other way.
Base-rate fallacyAccuracy misleads when the event is rare.
Precision–recall trade-offCutting one kind of error raises the other.
Threshold as policyThe cut-off is a choice, not a property of the model.
Discrimination vs calibrationRanking power (AUC) and accurate probabilities are separate tests.
Cost-sensitive decision ruleThe optimal cut-off, 1 / (1 + k), is set by the ratio of error costs.
Asymmetric payoff of debtCapped upside, open downside: why lenders are cautious.
Risk-adjusted pricingA loan must cover expected loss and the cost of capital.
Appendix · concepts 2 of 2

Ideas to take away

ConceptIn one lineSlide
Selection biasThe bank learns only from the loans it made.
Algorithmic fairnessAverage accuracy can hide disparity across groups.
Concept drift (dataset shift)Models degrade when the world changes.
Automation biasA machine's label shifts human decisions.
Non-delegable accountabilityThe person who signs answers for the AI's output.
Law as a constraint on AISome uses are high-risk by law and require explainability and human oversight (AI Act).
AI washingAsk first whether anything is actually being predicted.
Adoption–effectiveness gapBanks adopt AI where it is sold, not always where it works.
Framing effectLabels should not move judgment; evidence should.
Outcome biasJudge decisions by what was known, and models by calibration.
Three owners of a decisionThe AI predicts, the board sets k, the banker decides.

Appendix · ESG ecosystem 2 of 4

Rule-makers, supervisors, assurance

Rule-makers
European CommissionAdopts the EU rules: CSRD, ESRS, EU Taxonomy, SFDR, EU Green Bond StandardBook names the rules, §13.11.2
EFRAGDrafts the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS); technical adviser, not a regulator
ISSB (IFRS Foundation)Global sustainability disclosure standards; absorbed the TCFD's workBook, §13.11.4
Basel CommitteePrinciples for managing climate-related financial risk in banks
GHG Protocol · PCAFHow to count emissions (scopes) and a bank's financed emissions
GRI · SASBVoluntary reporting standards: impact (GRI), industry-specific (SASB, now ISSB)Book, §13.11.3–4
Supervisors
FinanstilsynetDanish FSA: supervises banks, including ESG and climate risk managementBook (AI governance context)
ErhvervsstyrelsenDanish Business Authority: company reporting law, including CSRD
Danmarks NationalbankFinancial stability, climate stress testing
EBAEU banking authority: ESG-risk guidelines, Pillar 3 ESG disclosures (Green Asset Ratio)
ESMAEU markets authority: credit rating agencies and, under new EU rules, ESG rating providers
EIOPAEU insurance and pensions authority: climate risk in insurers' solvency rules (Solvency II)
NGFSNetwork of central banks and supervisors: climate scenarios for stress tests
Assurance
External auditorsLimited assurance on the CSRD sustainability statement (e.g. Deloitte, EY, KPMG, PwC)Book, §13.11.2

Landscape as of autumn 2026; rules are changing quickly (EU Omnibus simplification, new ESG ratings regulation). Verify before relying on details.
